item.title: PopMelodyGen: A Copyright-Aware Platform for Controllable Pop-Melody Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.28686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-scale redistributable symbolic pop-melody data remain scarce due to copyright restrictions, creating a bottleneck for both practical deployment and reproducible research in music generation. We present PopMelodyGen, a copyright-aware platform for controllable pop-melody generation that combines rule-based synthesis with neural generation. Our approach first uses an expert synthesizer to produce large-scale labeled synthetic melodies from explicit musical knowledge and templates, providing scalable pretraining data with auditable provenance. A neural model is then pretrained on this corpus and adapted with a small licensed real-pop corpus to improve melodic naturalness while preserving controllability. The platform supports interactive melody creation with accompaniment playback and export for creators, as well as batch construction of annotated symbolic datasets for researchers. PopMelodyGen demonstrates a practical training and deployment paradigm for creative AI when large-scale reusable real-world data are limited.
item.dc:creator: Di Lu, Xinran Zhang, Qingwen Zhou, Yan Gao, Yuan Zhang, Xiaoqing Wang, Yuming Sun, Xiaobing Li, Maosong Sun

item.title: Training speech deepfake detectors against worst-case filters: Gains, Costs and Limits
item.description: arXiv:2611.28718v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speech deepfake detectors make few errors on standard benchmarks, yet a simple attack defeats them: the attacker passes fake speech through one short filter, tuned against the detector, and many fakes then pass as real. Training with random filters does not stop this attack, because the attacker uses the worst filter, not a random one. We therefore train the detector against the worst case: during training, a small set of filters is updated to fool the current detector, at about the cost of random filters. In a preregistered study, this made the detector more robust to filter attacks on real-world recordings than random filters did. It also lowered the in-domain attack error of the standard detector, and beat one-step adversarial training with additive noise on real-world recordings. The price is a higher error on unfiltered speech, and a validation study shows that choosing the checkpoint on held-out spoofing systems made the standard detector about as robust.
item.dc:creator: Ali Alavi

item.title: Beyond File-Level Splits: Rethinking Symbolic Music Evaluation via Multi-View Alignment
item.description: arXiv:2611.28765v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Symbolic music generation often continues MIDI passages by predicting subsequent notes or events. Held-out prediction loss can overestimate generalization to unseen compositions when training contains another performance or arrangement of a test work. We introduce Multi-View Alignment-Aware Same-Work Identification, combining complementary musical representations with temporal alignment of shared passages to remove test-work versions from training while preserving unrelated material and fixing evaluation files. In a controlled cohort of 100 manually verified pairs selected for high embedding similarity, replacing 3.29% of training windows with test-work versions reduces mean per-group NLL by up to 30.16% relative to matched unrelated content. Across two datasets and two generators, our method brings test losses closest to a reference built from independent work labels. Compared with removing the same number of files at random, it leaves fewer test works exposed and retains more eligible content, including about 99% of eligible tokens on the piano-performance dataset. A separate study on that dataset matches training tokens and updates: no test works remain exposed under the dataset labels, and mean relative test loss is 2.15% higher than an independently selected reference. These findings support keeping all versions of each composition in one split when evaluating generalization to unseen works. The project is available at https://kunbai05-nb.github.io/.
item.dc:creator: Kun Bai, Yinghan Wang, Canran Xiao, Jiachen Luo, Huy Phan, Yong Dai, Jiaqi Zhang, Yunwei Li, Lin Wang, Joshua Reiss, Bj\"orn W. Schuller

item.title: Restorable Multilingual Voice Anonymization via Audio Watermarking
item.description: arXiv:2611.28863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Voice anonymization aims to conceal speaker identity while preserving linguistic and paralinguistic information. However, certain applications also require the ability to attribute anonymized recordings to their original speakers. Existing recovery approaches often rely on specially designed reversible anonymization systems, limiting their applicability to different anonymization architectures. In this work, we propose a post-hoc framework for restorable multilingual voice anonymization that enables speaker attribution without reconstructing the original waveform or modifying the underlying anonymization systems. Specifically, we convert 192-dimensional speaker embeddings into binary identity payloads through sign quantization and embed them into anonymized speech using a segment-wise audio watermarking strategy. Recovered payloads are subsequently matched against enrollment speaker templates for identity attribution. We evaluate the framework across four languages using two distinct anonymization backbones, BM1 and T24. Under clean conditions, the approach achieves approximately 99% exact payload recovery and 0.96% attribution EER while largely preserving the original privacy-utility performance. Experiments further show that speaker attribution remains reliable under several audio distortions despite imperfect payload recovery, although temporal rescaling severely disrupts recovery. Additional analyses reveal that watermark robustness varies across languages, carrier durations, and anonymization backbones.
item.dc:creator: Haoyuan Zheng, Guang Hua, Xiaoxiao Miao

item.title: From Spatial Perception to Speech Recovery: Binaural Semantic Adaptation for Spatially Grounded Multi-Talker Transcription
item.description: arXiv:2611.29012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatial audio large language models increasingly combine general audio understanding with spatial perception. Yet overlapping conversations require more than locating speakers. A model must also recover what each person says and match the words to their positions. We examine this challenge in MiDashengLM-Spatial, a binaural model designed for both spatial reasoning and general audio understanding. To test these abilities, we introduce BiCP-Bench, a benchmark of overlapping two-speaker binaural recordings that contrasts candidate-based recognition, position-guided transcription, and joint transcription with spatial attribution. The model can identify a target utterance among candidates but struggles to transcribe it without them. Its semantic encoder uses only one ear. Changing that ear shifts which side's speech is recovered more accurately, despite unchanged binaural input to the spatial branch. We therefore propose Binaural Semantic Adaptation (BiSA), which combines shared encoding of both ears with cross-ear differential interactions. With the backbone frozen and 0.027% trainable parameters, BiSA raises correctly attributed joint transcription success from 0% to 57.81% for simultaneous onsets. For staggered onsets, later-speaker word error rate falls from 109.47% to 29.58%. On full-length Clarity CEC1 mixtures, word error rate falls from 59.33% to 39.60%. Spatial reasoning on MMAU-Pro improves by 9.54 percentage points without updating the spatial encoder, and general audio performance remains largely intact.
item.dc:creator: Wenxuan He, Shan Liang

item.title: Spoof Localization as Boundary Regression
item.description: arXiv:2611.29085v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Partially spoofed audio embeds spoofed segments in a bonafide utterance, and spoof localization is the task of locating them. Most countermeasures (CMs) operate at the frame level. Typically, they include a front-end representing the audio as frames and a back-end classifying each frame as bonafide or spoof. Such frame-level detection ties the reference, the predictions and the evaluation to a pre-defined temporal resolution: a frame containing a transition receives a single label, a boundary cannot lie inside a frame, and the evaluation also depends on the resolution. To tackle these issues, we treat spoof localization as regression. We propose a single-stage boundary regressor that outputs (start-time, end-time, score) tuples with continuous-valued time stamps, trained on the exact reference intervals. Results show that the proposed CM outperforms previous frame-level and boundary-based CMs, and generalizes better.
item.dc:creator: Yixuan Xiao, Xin Wang, Yassine El Kheir, Feidi Kallel, Arnab Das, Tim Polzehl, Sebastian M\"oller, Ngoc Thang Vu

item.title: IteraSong: LLM-Guided Iterative Symbolic Music Creation in a Web DAW
item.description: arXiv:2611.29225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Music creation is inherently iterative, yet many symbolic generation systems still center on producing or regenerating isolated outputs. We present IteraSong, an interactive web-based Digital Audio Workstation (DAW) for LLM-guided iterative symbolic music creation. Unlike one-shot generation systems, IteraSong supports a generate-audition-edit-refine loop over a persistent multi-track project. Users initialize a fully labeled pop draft, then progressively refine it through natural-language instructions. The LLM maps requests to a hierarchical action space of editing primitives exposed via Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, spanning global, track, section, and bar/note scopes. The demo enables attendees to edit multi-track compositions in natural language, apply deterministic and generative edits, and undo/redo changes in real time.
item.dc:creator: Di Lu, Xinran Zhang, Yan Gao, Yuan Zhang, Xiaoqing Wang, Qingwen Zhou, Xiaobing Li, Maosong Sun

item.title: Tenlai-TTS 2.0: Continuous-Representation LLM-Based TTS System with End-to-End Training
item.description: arXiv:2611.29226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autoregressive text-to-speech (TTS) with continuous speech latents avoids quantization-induced information loss, but typically relies on a latent space that is learned separately and then frozen before language-model training. Such a space must satisfy two competing requirements: it must retain enough acoustic detail for high-fidelity reconstruction, yet be sufficiently structured and regularized to support autoregressive prediction by a language model. We present Tenlai-TTS 2.0, which learns continuous speech representations through end-to-end training to balance acoustic detail with autoregressive predictability. The model comprises a speech encoder with a capacity-controlled Gaussian bottleneck, a large language model (LLM) with an autoregressive diffusion transformer (AR-DiT) head, a flow-matching (FM) mel-spectrogram decoder, and a multi-task recognition model (RM). With energy normalization and fixed-variance Gaussian noise, the bottleneck has a closed-form upper bound on its information rate. Through joint optimization with reconstruction, recognition, and next-patch prediction objectives, we learn continuous speech representations that suit all three tasks and train the LLM and AR-DiT for autoregressive generation. The LLM and AR-DiT are further optimized using differentiable reconstruction and recognition feedback on their predicted latents through the FM decoder and RM. On Seed-TTS-eval, this feedback-based optimization reduces character error rate (CER) from 0.82% to 0.74% on test-zh and from 8.32% to 7.08% on test-hard-zh, and word error rate (WER) from 1.32% to 1.27% on test-en, compared with joint training alone. Subsequent reinforcement learning further reduces CER to 6.29% on test-hard-zh and WER to 1.08% on test-en, with speaker similarity scores of 0.811, 0.766, and 0.784 on test-zh, test-en, and test-hard-zh, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Changfeng Gao, Yong Ren, Jun Yuan, Zhengkun Tian, Ye Bai, Zhao You, Shidong Shang

item.title: ARRANGE: Agentic Skills for Layering Vocals
item.description: arXiv:2611.29283v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adding a singing voice to an existing piano recording requires decisions about melody, syllable placement, pronunciation, timing, and vocal register. ARRANGE organizes this work as a sequence of agent skills with readable intermediate artifacts and composer approval checkpoints. An LLM translates instructions in plain English, notes played on a keyboard, and vocal references into local edits; deterministic scripts validate and apply those edits before open audio models render the result. The Score Canvas makes note, syllable, and pronunciation decisions inspectable and editable. In a benchmark of 16 revision requests, three draws per request, and five LLMs, typed edits achieved exact-change correctness of 0.83-0.98, compared with 0.33-0.69 for whole-plan rewriting without ARRANGE instructions. A separate score-editing benchmark and a first-person worked example examine the interaction between representations and corrections. Author listening evaluations further explore voice transfer and register selection, including 185 listening presentations across eight copied voices. These evaluations support the value of constrained editing and expose limits of both model execution and listening measures. The contribution is an interaction architecture for retaining musical decisions through inspectable intermediate representations, rather than a new singing model or evidence of general usability.
item.dc:creator: Henry Tan, Eidee Tan

item.title: SWIFT: A Handcrafted, Arithmetic-Minimal FPGA Engine for Real-Time Audio Deepfake Detection
item.description: arXiv:2611.29315v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative voice cloning threatens voice-based authentication, yet current deepfake detectors rely on power-hungry, high-precision models unsuited to edge hardware. We present SWIFT (Streaming Whiten-Integer Forensic Trust-Engine), a handcrafted detector that works in the high-frequency noise domain where synthesis artifacts concentrate. A first-order integer high-pass residual drives nine families of fixed-point descriptors, among them integer lifting-wavelet cepstral quantiles, Mahalanobis anomaly distances, Poincar\'e phase-space geometry, and phase jitter, fused by calibrated gradient-boosted trees and a sparse L1-regularised meta-learner. Under leakage-controlled nested cross-validation, with one shared preprocessing chain for real and fake audio, this reference model reaches accuracy of up to 99.86% and an Equal Error Rate (EER) as low as 0.03% across eight benchmarks. Its integer front-end and a fixed-point linear classifier run on the programmable logic of a PYNQ-Z2 (Zynq-7020) board, with a 7.85 microseconds per-frame datapath latency (127.4k frames/s) at 1.734 W and 11.2% LUT utilisation. Integer-only audio deepfake feature extraction is thus feasible at the edge without pretrained neural models or floating-point units.
item.dc:creator: Chirantan Banerjee, Soumita Chatterjee, Bhargab B. Bhattacharya, Hafizur Rahaman

item.title: MusicListenBench: Can Audio LLMs Hear the Difference Yet?
item.description: arXiv:2611.29375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Audio large language models (LLMs) are typically evaluated on song genre, mood, and instrumentation. A more basic skill is telling whether two short clips play the same melody, chord or instrument. We introduce MusicListenBench, a benchmark of paired listening tests for melody, harmony, timbre, and tempo. Each test item comes with two variants. A FLIP variant changes the music, so the answer must change. A STAY variant changes only the sound, such as room echo or hiss, so the answer must stay the same. The two variants have opposite answers, so a model that ignores the audio scores 50%, whatever letter it prefers. The benchmark has a training split and two test sets, one rendered from symbolic music with exact labels and one built from real recordings. On the rendered test, seven of eight open audio LLMs score within 4 points of this floor. Of four commercial models, both GPT-Audio models are at chance, and the best, Gemini 2.5 Pro, reaches 74.2%, 12.8 points below human listeners (87.0%). Post-training with GRPO on 10k rendered clean pairs raises Qwen2.5-Omni from 61.2% to 99.0% on held-out clean pairs, and the gain transfers to a task left out of training. On FLIP/STAY, however, it only reaches the level of our listeners (86.0%). It now misses almost no change (1.9%, against 24.7% for Gemini 2.5 Pro), yet when only the sound changes, it turns a correct answer into a wrong one 25.7\% of the time. More than half of its false flips come from a quiet background hiss. Models learn to hear a difference much faster than they learn which differences matter. On real recordings, open models again stay near chance, and the trained model calls 27 of 42 pairs of two strums of the same chord different. Adding sound-only pairs to training lowers false flips on both test sets, but no training run teaches relative pitch. We release the data, code, and an open leaderboard.
item.dc:creator: Abhinaba Roy, Ambuj Mehrish, Dorien Herremans

item.title: Who Plays What: Same-Instrument Music Separation from Video
item.description: arXiv:2611.29411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When two musicians in an ensemble play the same instrument, they sound alike and their instruments look alike. Audio-only separators, and audio-visual separators that rely on appearance, cannot tell them apart. What still differs is how each player moves, and when. We study same-instrument per-player separation: a user clicks one musician in a video and receives that musician's sound alone, even when other players in the video play the same instrument. Our model follows the clicked player and describes them with high level video features and the velocities of body and hand keypoints. A pretrained music separator attends to these tokens through cross-attention. Earlier motion-based separators were scored only on synthetic mixtures of solo videos. We give the first per-player evaluation of same-instrument separation on real ensemble recordings. On 58 players in URMP, each sharing an instrument with at least one other player in the piece, our model reaches a median SDR of 5.3 dB, while four released separators, audio-only and audio-visual, stay at or below 0.3 dB. The gap is wider on same-instrument duets, and our model also beats the audio-visual baselines on their own MUSIC benchmark. Tests show that the gain comes from movement: replacing the video with a still frame removes it, and so does shifting the video by a fraction of a second against the audio.
item.dc:creator: Abhinaba Roy, Ambuj Mehrish, Sebastiano Vascon, Dorien Herremans

item.title: Music Circuit: Trace and Control Style Dynamics in Large Music Generation Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.29475v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Musical style, a global attribute that functions throughout a whole piece, is a lever widely used by users in modern large music generation models. Yet how style is represented inside these models, and which components drive it, remains largely unexplored. In language models, circuit analysis traces a representation to a sparse sub-network of a few key components, namely attention heads and MLP neurons, and has been used successfully to explain and control global attributes such as emotion. In this work, we use circuit analysis to study the mechanisms behind musical style. Based on YuE2, we build a dataset that pairs the same lyrics with five styles and design a three-step framework. First, stage localization shows that the style forms mainly in the score-planning stage. Second, static observation across the positions of this stage further reveals that style is not a fixed vector but a dynamic representation across tokens. Third, we therefore merge the activation differences across positions into one direction per style, and trace the neurons and attention heads that drive this direction into a sparse circuit. Without any style text, steering this circuit successfully transfers one piece into the target style, matching and even exceeding the style prompt. To our knowledge, this is the first work to analyze and control musical style at the circuit level in a large music generation model. Audio and score examples are available at https://aristo233.github.io/Music_Circuit/.
item.dc:creator: Ruiji Yu, Wenye Ma, Gus Xia

item.title: Scoring L2 Pronunciation Without Synthesis: Counterfactual Velocity Contrast in Frozen Flow-Matching TTS
item.description: arXiv:2611.29985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Flow-matching text-to-speech (TTS) models learn how native speakers realize a text, yet this knowledge is used only for synthesis. We show that a frozen TTS model can score non-native (L2) pronunciation without generating audio. For a learner utterance, we compare the model's velocity-prediction error under the target text with its error under a counterfactual text (dropped or swapped) on the same noised input; the difference behaves like a generative goodness-of-pronunciation score. The signal is confined to a narrow band of high-noise timesteps, which a native-speech criterion locates and a closed-form rule transfers across backbones. On speaker-disjoint speechocean762, four frozen TTS models reach $r{=}0.58$--$0.63$ with human scores, within the range of zero-shot ASR and phone-level baselines, and adding them to those baselines in a label-free fusion raises $r$ from $0.698$ to $0.757$. Cached frame scores also flag word-level errors at no extra TTS cost.
item.dc:creator: Zehan Liu

item.title: AIRPiano: Piano Score Following with Tabletop Hand Gestures
item.description: arXiv:2611.30049v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AIRPiano aims to bring sound to the common practice of rehearsing piano music on a tabletop. Guided by a known score, users make piano-like finger movements on a flat surface without reproducing absolute keyboard positions. The score supplies pitches, while hand motion determines which score events to play and when. We formulate this interaction as online alignment between tabletop hand motion and symbolic score events. To address the ambiguity of tabletop motion, its differences from piano-playing motion, and the scarcity of aligned motion-score data, we develop motion and score representations, build a data processing pipeline, and train a Transformer with supervised attention on existing piano performance recordings. We further design a streaming inference framework that combines local alignment predictions with sequence tracking for real-time interaction. We construct two evaluation sets, VSF-Piano and VSF-Tabletop, to assess alignment on piano and tabletop performances, respectively. After a post-hoc global timing adjustment, AIRPiano achieves a mean chord alignment rate of 74% within a 133 ms tolerance on the paired subset of VSF-Tabletop, compared with 79% on VSF-Piano.
item.dc:creator: Jinxuan Zhu, Zhiyao Duan

item.title: SonicRender: Structured and Time-Grounded Rendering of Multi-Event Audio Scene Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.30241v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While unified audio generators can synthesize speech, music, and sound effects within a single model, producing a plausible mixture is only part of the challenge: a complex scene request also specifies which events occur, who produces them, and when they are heard. To satisfy these compositional constraints in a single generation pass, we present SonicRender, a unified multi-event audio renderer. Its Temporal Audio Scene Graph (TASG) binds persistent source identities to localized speech, music, ambience, and sound-effect events, together with their content, acoustic roles, relations, and timestamped windows. We further introduce AbsTime, which supplies the audio latent stream with absolute-frame coordinates and valid-canvas duration. Through joint text-audio attention and conditional flow matching, the renderer learns to realize structured, timed scenes as coherent mixtures. On the MMAG timestamp benchmark, SonicRender achieves speech/sound F1 scores of 0.79/0.60, exceeding the strongest reported scores in our comparison. On our SceneMix evaluation, it attains 85.4% all-event recall, 83.9% window-hit rate, and 95.7% speaker accuracy. Subjective study further demonstrates significant improvements over all five comparison systems in both perceived audio quality and scene realization. Results across speech, general audio, music, multi-event load, and temporal-grounding analyses establish precise, composition-aware audio rendering within a unified generator. Demo page: https://caiyunrui.github.io/SonicRender.
item.dc:creator: Yunrui Cai, Xu Li, Yan Rong, Dingdong Wang, Yucheng Zhou, Xixin Wu, Chen Zhang, Zhiyong Wu, Helen Meng

item.title: LiveAudio: From Bidirectional to Autoregressive Diffusion for Real-Time Streaming Video-to-Audio Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.30714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Video-to-audio generation synthesizes sound that matches a video in content and timing, with applications ranging from film post-production to live streaming, games and interactive world models. Interactive applications receive video continuously and need the sound to follow it in real time, yet most existing video-to-audio models are bidirectional and must observe an entire clip before producing any sound. We propose LiveAudio, a streaming video-to-audio framework that generates high-quality and synchronized audio in real time while the video is playing. In contrast to prior streaming models trained from scratch, LiveAudio converts a bidirectional model into a streaming generator so as to build on its audio quality and synchronization. LiveAudio generates audio block by block, and each block depends only on the video that has already been played. The streaming generator is obtained from the bidirectional model through progressive causal fine-tuning and distillation, so that each block needs only a few sampling steps. Experiments on VGGSound show that LiveAudio outperforms existing streaming models in audio quality and synchronization, and surpasses the bidirectional model it starts from in synchronization. On a single A100 GPU, it runs in real time with a real-time factor of 0.79 and a time to first frame of 143 ms. Audio samples are available at https://streamaudio.github.io.
item.dc:creator: Yuxuan Jiang, Zehua Chen, Yusheng Dai, Andong Wang, Weibei Dou, Jun Zhu

item.title: What Do Sound Event Embeddings Reveal? Auditing Speaker Leakage in Audio Representations
item.description: arXiv:2611.31043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pretrained audio embeddings are increasingly used as intermediate representations for sound event detection (SED) and other always-on acoustic sensing tasks. While these representations are selected for their utility on downstream tasks, they may also retain sensitive information unrelated to their intended purpose, creating privacy risks even when raw audio is not exposed. In this work, we present an empirical framework for auditing privacy leakage from pretrained audio embeddings using two complementary approaches. First, we quantify representation-level leakage by measuring statistical dependence between an audio embedding and a representation specialized for encoding sensitive information. Second, we measure attack-level leakage by training lightweight adversarial probes to recover sensitive attributes directly from the embedding. We apply this framework to four widely used audio representations (CLAP, PANNs, AST, and YAMNet) and evaluate leakage of speaker identity and gender. We found that speaker identification balanced accuracy ranges from $0.43$ to $0.72$, while gender information is also strongly recoverable. Moreover, representation-level and attack-based measurements exhibit consistent trends, with CLAP leaking the most and YAMNet leaking the lest speaker identity. These results demonstrate that intermediate audio representations are not inherently privacy-preserving interfaces and motivate privacy leakage as an explicit criterion, alongside downstream utility, when selecting representations for acoustic sensing systems.
item.dc:creator: Bhawana Chhaglani

item.title: CAST: A Deployed Speech-to-Text Cascade for Closed Captioning of Entertainment Television
item.description: arXiv:2611.31055v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite rapid progress in automatic speech recognition (ASR), caption generation for long-form entertainment video remains challenging for content dense in music and effects, rich in accents, crosstalk, and noise. The transcript quality depends on segmentation and surrounding modules as much as the acoustic model. A single pass voice activity detection (VAD) can miss faint, low-energy voice while forwarding near-silent segments that induce hallucination and repetition in an autoregressive decoder. These competing errors motivate a hierarchical VAD that revisits rejected segments under semantic and acoustic retention checks. We present Captioning ASR Stack for Television (CAST), an integrated speech-to-text pipeline for closed captioning (CC) combining frozen Whisper large-v3 with segmentation, language identification, lyrics routing, and targeted hallucination detection and repair on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU. On 100 in-house assets spanning 60.46 hours, CAST reduces normalized WER from 6.99% to 5.36% and subtitle edit rate from 254.2 to 221.9 min/hour against the WhisperX pipeline, and improves deletion rate by 11% on public datasets. We also present the behavior of each stage in the pipeline. CAST entered the production speech-to-text (STT) stage of our CC pipeline in late August 2026; we report the evaluation evidence and path to full-scale operation.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Mishra, Thanish Bolla, Bidisha Sharma, Balaji Pitchaikannu, Surbhi Sinha, Anup Kotalwar

item.title: SoundFleXR: Selectively Constraining Axes of Audio Rendering Presentations
item.description: arXiv:2611.28020v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Extended reality (XR) systems increasingly rely on audio cues to help users locate, interpret, and interact with virtual content, especially when the content is outside the field of view. To support this, many systems use head-related transfer functions (HRTFs) to approximate real-world acoustics. However, a realistic simulation is only one possible presentation. Audio can also be altered by constraining, flexing, or contracting the spatial dimensions represented in the signal. This work examines how selectively constraining or flexing the number of audio dimensions affects localization performance across XR task structures with different spatial degrees of freedom. We compare two-channel spatial audio, azimuth-only HRTF, and full HRTF rendering across orientation-based (3DoF) and translation-based (6DoF) tasks. Azimuth-only HRTF was mutually non-inferior to full HRTF for total angular error across task conditions, including at the strictest tested tolerance in 3DoF (5 degrees), and remained comparable for azimuth error at (10 degrees) and larger tolerances in both 3DoF and 6DoF. In contrast, two-channel stereo required coarser tolerances to reach non-inferiority, becoming comparable to full HRTF for 6DoF azimuth error at (15 degrees) but not (10 degrees). From these comparisons, we derive design lessons and application scenarios that indicate when fewer spatial cues provide sufficient support and when richer spatial cues are beneficial.
item.dc:creator: Brandon Woodard, Hyunju Kim, Hyunsung Cho, David Lindlbauer, Rhonda Wilson, Joseph LaViola Jr

item.title: NAVIQUAL-XR: Finding the Sweet Spot of a Live Music Environment in Augmented Reality
item.description: arXiv:2611.28056v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Augmented Reality (AR) enables immersive spatial audio experiences that extend conventional stereo and head-tracked listening to six degrees-of-freedom (6-DoF) navigation. However, evaluating listener Quality of Experience (QoE) remains a key challenge due to the real-time and dynamic adaptations of the content in AR environments. To address this challenge, we propose NAVIQUAL-XR, an objective model to find the "sweet spot" in AR live music environments validated by subjective tests. We recruited 25 listeners who navigated 12 AR environments of various scene set ups under auditory and audio-visual modalities. We analyzed their navigation trajectories and recorded their final locations and directions as their subjective sweet spots. We then produced subjective maps that identified the location and direction with the optimal QoE in an AR environment. Furthermore, we benchmarked key objective metrics that predict these sweet spots through similarity metrics with the subjective maps. We found that localization quality derived from BINAQUAL, an objective metric designed for binaural audio, outperformed signal-to-noise ratio in closely predicting the sweet spot. This suggests that phase-based cues play a more important role on perceived QoE in AR environments than intensity-based cues. NAVIQUAL-XR provides new insights into listener behavior and preferences in AR environments, demonstrating the potential of objective metrics to predict the subjective experience, and guiding the design of future immersive audio systems.
item.dc:creator: Carl Timothy Tolentino, Andrew Hines

item.title: LightOnOCR for AMNLT: Reading Chant Notation and Lyrics in One Pass, from Single Staves to Whole Pages
item.description: arXiv:2611.28094v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Aligned music notation and lyrics transcription (AMNLT) asks for the notes of a chant, its sung text and the assignment of syllables to notes in one output. Fuentes-Mart\'inez et al., who defined the task, found that the one vision-language model they tested fell far behind specialised recognisers. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B, a page OCR model with one billion parameters, end to end, vision encoder included, to write a staff as a GABC string whose letters denote staff positions. Trained on the published AMNLT training split alone, it more than halves the best published aligned music and lyrics error rate (AMLER) on Solesmes, the one directly comparable dataset (9.9 against 21.0 %); on Einsiedeln and Salzinnes, measured in a different encoding, its figures are also lower. The benchmark does not measure generalisation to unseen manuscripts: while the pitch error on AMNLT validation stays between 1.7 and 1.9 %, on 200 staves from five unseen manuscripts it falls from 24.9 to 1.3 % as we add chant aligned through CantusDB, Transkribus ground truth and silver staves kept only where two readers agree. Trained also on multi-staff images, it reads whole pages without staff detection (pitch error 3.3 to 3.8 % on validation and test pages, 1.9 % on pages of unseen manuscripts). Remaining errors include Gothic F clefs read as C clefs, notes dropped with abbreviated or illegible text and lower accuracy on pages with small notation. Controlled ablations are needed to explain the gains.
item.dc:creator: Robert Klugseder (Austrian Centre for Digital Humanities)

item.title: Beyond Raw IQ: Compact Semantic Representations for Task Oriented Automatic Modulation Classification
item.description: arXiv:2611.28813v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automatic modulation classification (AMC) is an important component of modern wireless communication systems, but conventional signal representations can be expensive to store, process, and communicate, particularly under noisy channel conditions. This work investigates whether learned semantic representations can provide a compact alternative to high-dimensional in-phase and quadrature (IQ) representations while retaining robustness to noise. Starting from a 2048-dimensional IQ representation, we evaluate learned semantic representations with dimensions of 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64. Across the evaluated configurations, a 16-dimensional representation provides the strongest overall trade-off between classification performance, robustness, and representation size. The resulting representation achieves a 128x compression ratio and a 99.22% reduction in dimensionality. We further evaluate representation stability across signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), compare semantic representations with a raw-IQ CNN, analyze per-class robustness, and perform five-seed validation. The five-seed evaluation produces an average accuracy of (49.22 +- 0.52)% and Macro-F1 of (49.27 +- 0.53)% across the evaluated SNR range. These results indicate that learned semantic compression can produce a substan- tially smaller representation while preserving useful classification information and improving geometric stability under noise.
item.dc:creator: Omm Swarup, Shrishail M. Hiremath

item.title: When Being Wrong Is Right: Reverse-Capability Audio CAPTCHAs through Psychoacoustic Design
item.description: arXiv:2611.28823v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) have recently been shown to bypass audio CAPTCHAs designed around limitations of automatic speech recognition. To address this threat, we introduce reverse-capability verification, a general CAPTCHA framework that reverses the conventional human-easy, machine-hard relationship with respect to the physical ground truth. It selects challenges in which stable human perceptual limitations cause the human-reference answer to differ from the physical ground truth, while machine analysis tends toward that truth. Because the verifier accepts the human-reference answer, advanced solver capabilities and resulting improved recovery of the physical ground truth may instead strengthen the human-machine separation. We instantiate the framework through psychoacoustics and design two audio CAPTCHAs: HIPI, a classification task, and YINGCHEN, a counting task, together with their conjunctive composition. Across seven LALMs and eight attack strategies, the maximum observed machine acceptance rates are 19%, 17%, and 3% for HIPI, YINGCHEN, and their composition, respectively, compared with 45-100% for nine prior schemes. A multidimensional human usability study yields corresponding human acceptance rates of 78%, 90%, and 76%, while maintaining competitive efficiency and satisfaction. Further analysis demonstrates that advanced LALMs tend toward physical ground truth. These results show that reverse-capability verification substantially reduces machine acceptance while retaining high human acceptance through an approach different from conventional CAPTCHAs.
item.dc:creator: Mingjie Bao, Yu Dai, Guangke Chen, Guozhu Meng

item.title: StudioBench: Benchmarking Agentic Multimodal Large Language Models for Productive Audiovisual Creation
item.description: arXiv:2611.28902v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Video generators can now render convincing short clips, yet complete audiovisual works require coordinating visuals, sound, and editing across multiple stages. Existing benchmarks focus on individual generators or video agents under narrower production settings, leaving end-to-end creation by general multimodal large language models (MLLMs) underexplored. We introduce StudioBench, a benchmark comprising 160 tasks across eight video genres and five task types, spanning diverse audiovisual production requirements. Models produce minutes of finished audiovisual content using 33 atomic generation, editing, and inspection tools, without shell access or workflow templates. We evaluate the delivered films, while analyzing reconstructed workflow graphs to characterize production behavior and diagnose failures. Across seven MLLMs, explicit requirements are nearly saturated, yet production quality varies substantially in picture clarity and composition, object structure, motion, and lip sync. All models spontaneously organize multi-stage production workflows without predefined templates. However, higher-quality models exhibit more selective production workflows, whereas additional tool calls alone show little association with quality. These findings identify the missing quality loop of effective inspection, selection, and revision as a key bottleneck in productive audiovisual creation.
item.dc:creator: Xinglong Xu, Yuxia Zhu, Siyuan Li, Lixu Tian, Xiaofei Zhao, Yuxin Liu, Caijun Jia, Jintao Chen, Bihui Yu, Alden Cai, Asher Qin, Jingxuan Wei, Cheng Tan

item.title: CANDOR: A Multilingual Provenance-Documented Corpus for Dysarthric Speech Research
item.description: arXiv:2611.28930v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: CANDOR assembles 61 corpora across 17 languages and five aetiological classes plus a mixed/other group. Its register counts 2,057 speakers classified as dysarthric and 19,538 healthy controls. The collection contains 4,469.7 hours of audio, including 1,178.8 hours in the dysarthric subset. Counts use speech-impairment labels where available and diagnosis labels otherwise. The collection includes 732 dysarthric speakers across 14 non-English languages; 194 speakers use six languages unsupported by Qwen3-ASR, the model underlying its non-English baselines. We document composition, chain of custody, licences and transfer terms, while distinguishing corpus-level provenance from participant-level consent records, which we hold for few constituents. Among 31 dysarthric-bearing corpora, open licences cover 29.0% of corpora, 10.5% of speakers and 8.2% of hours. Excluding the English Speech Accessibility Project raises the open hour share to 31.2%, showing its dependence on this collection's composition. CANDOR cannot be redistributed as a single audio resource; we specify public, restricted and conditional artefacts. Severity labels available in 15 corpora do not provide a validated cross-corpus mapping. Within the non-English ASR baselines, only Mandarin yields a real-speech estimate meeting our evaluation criteria. It differs sharply from the synthesis result and remains imprecise; an English challenge result uses a different model and protocol. CANDOR provides a documented basis for research on under-represented languages while making constraints on evaluation, comparability and sharing explicit.
item.dc:creator: Bernard Muller, LaVonne Roberts, Leo Kaiya, Antonio Ortiz Barra\~n\'on

item.title: Speech Emotion Recognition Across Languages: Prosodic Patterns and Self-Supervised Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.29040v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This study investigates the prosodic patterns of emotional speech across Chinese (CN), German (DE), and English (EN), with a focus on acoustic characteristics. Using ANOVA and mixed-effects modeling, we reveal cross-linguistic and emotion-specific prosodic patterns. A comparative analysis of Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) performance demonstrates that humans outperform Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) models in cross-lingual tasks, while SSL models show significant improvement in cross-lingual SER through an efficient fine-tuning process, achieving performance competitive with native human speakers. The study also analyzes the performance of Speech Emotion Diarization (SED) between models and humans, highlighting the effectiveness of SSL models in transfer learning scenarios. These findings emphasize the interplay between universal prosodic features (e.g., intensity, pitch) and language-specific factors. Moreover, the SSL model's outstanding performance indicates the potential value of these acoustic features in emotion processing, implying possible advancements in cross-lingual emotion recognition through refined training techniques.
item.dc:creator: Tianqi Geng, Zhichen Han, Hui Feng, Jiahong Yuan, Korin Richmond, Yuanchao Li

item.title: PAWP-TTS: Phoneme-Aware Weight Programming for Compact Bilingual English-Nepali Speech Synthesis
item.description: arXiv:2611.29455v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper presents PAWP-TTS, a compact non-autoregressive text-to-speech system for English, Nepali, and English-Nepali code-mixed speech at 24 kHz, with no language model at inference. Deterministic pronunciation knowledge lives in a rule- and lexicon-based bilingual frontend that preserves native Nepali contrasts and avoids Hindi phonology, so the network only models acoustics. Counting every learned inference tensor, including the waveform decoder, PAWP-1.5M (1,490,390 parameters, 5.98 MB) reaches 1.50% English and 1.75% Nepali character error rate under a single ASR recognizer, and 5.04% / 4.02% Nepali / English phoneme error rate (PER) on 600 untouched test utterances. Decoder-centric 281K-parameter models (1.1 MB) stay intelligible across three independent seeds, with equal-budget dense models (5.53 +/- 0.08% NE, 5.34 +/- 0.28% EN PER) outperforming K=2 cross-layer shared-basis models (6.35 +/- 0.11% NE, 6.57 +/- 0.47% EN PER). Fixing a frontend/label version mismatch nearly halved Nepali PER, more than any architectural or weight-level change. The paper then studies weight-space programming: inspection-guided, zero-training weight edits. Under strict controls (validation-only selection, one-shot test, paired bootstrap, matched random and same-parameter gradient baselines), edits show real selectivity (27:1 on word-boundary pauses with 96 weights; zero cross-lingual collateral inside language-gated residuals) but no accuracy gain beyond controls. Two apparent targets proved to be label or phonology artifacts. Code, ONNX graphs, and CC BY 4.0 weights are released.
item.dc:creator: Firoj Paudel

item.title: Characterizing Frozen SSL Encoders and Backends for Cross-Domain Speech Deepfake Detection
item.description: arXiv:2611.29865v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) encoders are the dominant front end for speech deepfake detection, and the prevailing recipe fine-tunes the full encoder on a small spoofing corpus, maximizing in-domain accuracy at the cost of known degradation under domain shift. Taking a recent cross-attention fusion of SSL and constant-Q cepstral features as a fixed reference recipe, we freeze its encoder and ask which encoder and which backend behave best across domains. We cross two frozen encoders, the massively multilingual XEUS and Wav2Vec2 XLSR-53, with two backends, multi-head factorized attentive (MHFA) pooling and AASIST, and evaluate on ASVspoof 2019 LA, ASVspoof 2021 LA and DF, In-the-Wild (ITW), and ASVspoof 5, training every system in one pipeline over three seeds. We report three findings. First, encoder and backend interact: MHFA suits the stronger encoder, while AASIST recovers more from and stabilizes the weaker one. Second, within this recipe, the frozen encoder produces large, repeatable differences. With MHFA, frozen XEUS lowers error relative to frozen XLSR-53 by 58-77% on LA21, DF21, and ASV5, and more modestly on ITW. This ordering persists in a matched-aggregation ablation, and a capacity-matched WavLM Large diagnostic shows that parameter count alone does not explain XLSR-53's weaker performance. Third, against a three-seed fine-tuned baseline, frozen XEUS updates under 0.4M parameters versus 316M, wins on ASVspoof 5 (in EER and min-DCF) and modestly on LA21, trails on DF21 and ITW, and shows lower seed variation on three of the four out-of-domain sets.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Hurt, Oscar O'Donnell, Yefei Yang, Anjani Sethi, Priyanka Durai

item.title: Which Layer to Trust? Layer Selection in Frozen Speech Encoders for Singing-Voice Deepfake Detection under Signal Corruption
item.description: arXiv:2611.29871v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Frozen self-supervised speech encoders have been frequently used for audio deepfake detection. However, the layers are usually chosen from a development set. We examine this choice for singing-voice deepfake detection on CtrSVDD. We train one detection head per layer, plus a learned layer mix, on frozen XEUS (3-4 seeds) and XLS-R (2 seeds). We test on clean audio and under noise, reverberation and lossy coding. On clean audio, the middle layers beat the last layer in both encoders and the learned mix does not beat the best single layer. The layer chosen on the development set is 2.3 (XEUS) and 4.1 (XLS-R) percentage points of EER worse than the best test layer. Under noise and coding, XEUS's best layers stay in the middle, while under reverberation its upper layers catch up, whereas XLS-R's best layer moves shallower. In an exploratory analysis, XEUS detects a commercial synthesis attack best with an earlier layer, especially under noise. The layer therefore cannot be chosen reliably on an in-domain development set and clean audio alone.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Hurt, Yefei Yang

item.title: Ultrasound Watermark: Real-time Acoustic Watermarking against Voice Scams on Smartphones
item.description: arXiv:2611.30106v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent advances in text-to-speech (TTS), voice conversion (VC), and AI-driven speech synthesis enable adversaries to convincingly impersonate trusted individuals during phone calls. Existing defenses often rely on offline analysis, degrade under telephony distortions, or remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks. To address these limitations, we present Ultrasound Watermark, a real-time, smartphone-native framework that protects live calls by binding speech to the caller's physical articulatory motion through acoustic watermarking. During a call, the smartphone emits ultrasonic signals and captures reflections from facial articulatory movements using only its built-in speaker and microphone. Ultrasound Watermark extracts motion features from these reflections and fuses them with outgoing speech to generate a dynamic watermark. Because the ultrasonic measurements are physically and temporally coupled with speech production, they are difficult to spoof without the underlying articulatory motion. A synchronized generator-detector architecture enforces cross-modal speech-motion consistency against replay, synthesized speech, and articulation-mimicking attacks. Ultrasound Watermark operates continuously with less than 200 ms latency overhead and requires no additional hardware. We implement Ultrasound Watermark on iOS and Android and evaluate it using over 2.5 hours of synchronized speech-ultrasound recordings from 22 speakers across eight smartphones and four real-world environments. Results demonstrate robustness to diverse attacks and telephony distortions while preserving perceptual audio quality.
item.dc:creator: Renzhi Hao, Shirui Cao, Yizhu Wen, Rishav Gupta, Dharani Nadendla, Mehran Kafai, Hanqing Guo, Dong Li

item.title: Audio-Visual Rearrangement
item.description: arXiv:2611.30171v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce Audio-Visual Rearrangement (AVR), a novel task in which an agent hears a spoken request, retrieves a suitable object, and delivers it to the requesting user or an instruction-specified destination. AVR requires the agent to understand the spoken request and acoustically localize the speaker for delivery. To support this task, we construct a dataset covering three query types: explicit target specification, speaker-relative spatial references, and implicit user intent, spanning eight subtypes with diverse object selection and delivery requirements. Moreover, we propose a framework that integrates a motion-aware spatial audio module into an audio-visual large language model to encode spatial cues from the spoken request and update them as the agent moves. We further incorporate auxiliary supervision for speech understanding, spatial audio perception, and visual grounding through multitask instruction tuning to improve action prediction. Experiments establish baseline performance in both seen and unseen environments, laying the groundwork for future research on embodied intelligence and human-robot interaction. The code will be publicly available soon.
item.dc:creator: Ruohao Guo, Jiatong Ye, Chenwei Dong, Jinxing Zhou, Dantong Niu, Guangyao Li, Zhenbo Li

item.title: Synthetic Twins: Closing the Gap Between TTS Test Sets and Real Recordings in Turkish ASR Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2611.30694v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speech synthesized by text-to-speech engines is a low-cost substitute for recorded test sets in automatic speech recognition, yet an off-the-shelf synthetic test set is worth only a few dozen real recordings for estimating the real error rate of a recognizer. This paper examines which properties of real recordings are missing from synthetic speech and how much of the gap can be closed. For 507 Turkish Common Voice recordings, synthetic twins are built: a ladder of synthetic copies that adds, one factor at a time, the pitch of the speaker, a clone of the same speaker, the real recording channel and the speaking rate. At each step, the agreement between ASR behaviour on the copy and on the real recording is measured. Across three zero-shot cloning engines and panels of six and 19 recognizers, the speaker clone is the step that improves agreement on which sentences are hard, raising the Spearman correlation from .41 to .55 for Chatterbox. Matching the channel or adding generic noise corrects the error level when the synthetic speech is easier than real speech. The twin with the highest worth is equivalent to 70 to 122 real recordings, depending on the recognizer panel, compared with about 9 for a stock voice. The findings replicate on VoxForge, a second corpus in which speaker identity is known rather than inferred: the clone raises sentence agreement from .31 to .50 and the worth from 8 to about 50 recordings. Agreement on which sentences are hard is distinct from agreement on how hard they are. The paper concludes with a practical recipe and a reporting checklist for synthetic ASR test sets.
item.dc:creator: Nur Ya\u{g}mur Tuncer, Mustafa Serta\c{c} T\"urkel, Fatma Nur Korkmaz, Ahmet Tu\u{g}rul Bayrak

item.title: FGAS: Fixed Decoder Network-Based Audio Steganography with Adversarial Perturbation Generation
item.description: arXiv:2505.22266v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) has made high-fidelity generated audio widely available across the Internet, driving the advancement of audio steganography. Benefiting from advances in deep learning, current audio steganography schemes are mainly based on encoder-decoder network architectures. While these methods achieve promising perceptual quality, they typically require network pre-training, and maintaining anti-steganalysis performance at high payloads remains challenging. To address these issues, we propose Fixed Decoder Network-Based Audio Steganography with Adversarial Perturbation Generation (FGAS). Adversarial perturbations carrying a secret message are embedded into the cover audio to generate stego audio. The sender and receiver independently construct the same fixed decoder from a shared architecture and initialization key, avoiding the transfer of trained decoder parameters. In FGAS, we propose an Audio Adversarial Perturbation Generation (A2PG) strategy with an optional robust extension and design a lightweight fixed decoder. The fixed decoder guarantees reliable extraction of the hidden message, while adversarial perturbations are optimized to keep the stego audio perceptually and statistically close to the cover audio, thereby improving anti-steganalysis performance. The experimental results show that FGAS significantly improves stego audio quality, achieving an average PSNR gain of over 10 dB compared to SOTA methods. Furthermore, FGAS demonstrates strong robustness against common audio processing attacks. Moreover, FGAS exhibits superior anti-steganalysis performance across different relative payloads; under high-capacity embedding, it achieves a classification error rate about 2% higher, indicating stronger anti-steganalysis performance than current SOTA methods.
item.dc:creator: Jialin Yan, Yu Cheng, Zhaoxia Yin, Xinpeng Zhang, Shilin Wang, Tanfeng Sun, Xinghao Jiang

item.title: Rhythm-TTS: High-Fidelity Shortcut Latent Modeling and Probabilistic Rhythm Generation for Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech
item.description: arXiv:2510.02848v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) systems are commonly built on either discrete codec tokens or continuous acoustic representations. Discrete-token models benefit from stable sequence modeling and explicit speech factorization, but they ultimately synthesize speech through codebook lookup and codeword composition, which can accumulate errors and impose a quality ceiling on naturalness and speaker similarity. Continuous-representation models can generate fine-grained speech latents directly, but often require heavier in-context modeling and less explicit alignment. This paper presents Rhythm-TTS, a shortcut zero-shot TTS framework that combines the factorizability of discrete codec tokens with the fidelity of continuous latent generation. Instead of using predicted codec tokens as the final acoustic representation, Rhythm-TTS uses them as a semantic-acoustic prior and directly generates holistic continuous speech latents with flow matching, bypassing the discrete-to-latent reconstruction path at inference time. We further address an underexplored dimension of speech naturalness: rhythm diversity across multiple synthesis runs. Motivated by the hypothesis that rhythm variation is largely governed by phoneme duration changes and the occurrence of silent pauses, we introduce probabilistic Duration and Silence Generators to sample dynamic pacing patterns before acoustic generation. Experiments on zero-shot TTS benchmarks evaluate intelligibility, naturalness, speaker similarity, efficiency, and run-to-run rhythm diversity, showing that the proposed shortcut latent modeling and probabilistic rhythm generation improve the fidelity and temporal naturalness of non-autoregressive zero-shot TTS. Code and audio samples are available at our demo page https://rhythm-tts.github.io.
item.dc:creator: Hieu-Nghia Huynh-Nguyen, Ngoc-Son Nguyen, Long-Khanh Pham, Huynh Nguyen Dang, Huy Tien Nguyen, Van Nguyen

item.title: AlphaFlowTSE: One-Step Generative Target Speaker Extraction via Conditional AlphaFlow
item.description: arXiv:2603.10701v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Target speaker extraction (TSE) aims to recover the speech of a specified speaker from a multi-talker mixture using a short enrollment utterance from that speaker. Real conversational applications require both high extraction quality and low-latency inference across complex mixture conditions. Existing generative TSE approaches improve speech fidelity, but diffusion and flow-based models usually rely on multi-step sampling. One-step variants reduce iterative inference cost, yet often require estimating a trajectory coordinate related to the mixing ratio, introducing an additional dependency. We propose AlphaFlowTSE, which formulates TSE as finite-interval transport from the observed mixture to clean target speech. AlphaFlowTSE learns a conditional mean velocity along a mixture-to-target trajectory and uses a JVP-free AlphaFlow objective that combines local trajectory matching with interval-consistent teacher--student supervision. This parameterization supports predictor-free inference while remaining compatible with an optional MR-enabled configuration. At separator NFE$=1$, the MR-enabled configuration attains the highest PESQ, ESTOI, and SI-SDR among the compared one-step systems on Libri2Mix; under predictor-free inference on REAL-T PRIMARY, AlphaFlowTSE yields lower downstream ASR error rates and higher target-speaker similarity.
item.dc:creator: Duojia Li, Shuhan Zhang, Zihan Qian, Wenxuan Wu, Shuai Wang, Qingyang Hong, Lin Li, Haizhou Li

item.title: TRACE: Training-Free Partial Audio Deepfake Detection via Embedding Trajectory Analysis of Speech Foundation Models
item.description: arXiv:2604.01083v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Partial audio deepfakes, where synthesized segments are spliced into genuine recordings, are particularly deceptive because most of the audio remains authentic. Existing detectors are supervised: they require frame-level annotations, overfit to specific synthesis pipelines, and must be retrained as new generative models emerge. We argue that this supervision is unnecessary. We hypothesize that speech foundation models implicitly encode a forensic signal: genuine speech forms smooth, slowly varying embedding trajectories, while splice boundaries introduce abrupt disruptions in frame-level transitions. Building on this, we propose TRACE (Training-free Representation-based Audio Countermeasure via Embedding dynamics), a training-free framework that detects partial audio deepfakes by analyzing the first-order dynamics of frozen speech foundation model representations without any training, labeled data, or architectural modification. We evaluate TRACE on four benchmarks that span two languages using six speech foundation models. In PartialSpoof, TRACE achieves 8.08% EER, competitive with fine-tuned supervised baselines. In LlamaPartialSpoof, the most challenging benchmark featuring LLM-driven commercial synthesis, TRACE surpasses a supervised baseline outright (24.12% vs. 24.49% EER) without any target-domain data. These results show that temporal dynamics in speech foundation models provide an effective, generalize signal for training-free audio forensics.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) Workshops, pp. 7405 7414, 2026
item.dc:creator: Awais Khan, Muhammad Umar Farooq, Kutub Uddin, Khalid Malik

item.title: Dual-Branch Gated Fusion for Open-Set Audio Deepfake Source Tracing
item.description: arXiv:2606.10223v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Attributing a synthetic utterance to its originating system remains an open challenge: closed-set models fail to reject unseen synthesizers and produce overconfident predictions. To address this, we propose a dual-branch gated fusion framework that pairs XLSR-53 with CORES, a 66-dimensional descriptor that, unlike prior Linear Filter Bank (LFB)-only work, spans cepstral, oscillatory, rhythmic, energy, and spectral dimensions to capture complementary synthesis artifacts. Our analysis shows XLSR-53 remains discriminative in-domain (ID) while CORES generalizes stably under distribution shift (OOD), yet their naive concatenation fails due to SSL representational imbalance. To resolve this, an input-conditioned gate adaptively weights each branch under joint training with cross-entropy, an energy margin loss for ID/OOD separation, and a gate diversity term. On the MLAAD benchmark, our system achieves 97.6\% ID accuracy, 4.9\% EERc, and an 83.5\% relative FPR95 reduction over the Interspeech 2025 baseline.
item.dc:creator: Awais Khan, Kutub Uddin, Khalid Malik

item.title: Self-Distilled Pronunciation and Accent Control for Neural Text-to-Speech
item.description: arXiv:2609.17234v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Text-to-speech that reads raw text has no lexicon: a rare word is read as guessed, and a native Japanese listener accepts a word only if its reading and pitch accent are both right. A known remedy installs a reading-and-accent channel into a released model, but it needs many recordings. This paper removes the recordings: the frozen backbone reads a sentence containing a common word it already says correctly, and that output serves as the teacher for the same sentence with the word replaced by an annotated reading with its pitch accent. Screened raters judged the tag right on 0.80 to 0.93 of unseen difficult words on four backbones spanning autoregressive, diffusion, and encoder-decoder synthesis; plain kana, which cannot express an accent, got 0.38 to 0.60. On words needing no edit, naturalness is non-inferior on one backbone; on the other three, listeners prefer the unedited rendition by 0.19 to 0.26.
item.dc:creator: Shuhei Kato

item.title: SpA2V: Harnessing Spatial Auditory Cues for Audio-driven Spatially-aware Video Generation
item.description: arXiv:2508.00782v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Audio-driven video generation aims to synthesize realistic videos that align with input audio recordings, akin to the human ability to visualize scenes from auditory input. However, existing approaches predominantly focus on exploring semantic information, such as the classes of sounding sources present in the audio, limiting their ability to generate videos with accurate content and spatial composition. In contrast, we humans can not only naturally identify the semantic categories of sounding sources but also determine their deeply encoded spatial attributes, including locations and movement directions. This useful information can be elucidated by considering specific spatial indicators derived from the inherent physical properties of sound, such as loudness or frequency. As prior methods largely ignore this factor, we present SpA2V, the first framework explicitly exploits these spatial auditory cues from audios to generate videos with high semantic and spatial correspondence. SpA2V decomposes the generation process into two stages: 1) Audio-guided Video Planning: We meticulously adapt a state-of-the-art MLLM for a novel task of harnessing spatial and semantic cues from input audio to construct Video Scene Layouts (VSLs). This serves as an intermediate representation to bridge the gap between the audio and video modalities. 2) Layout-grounded Video Generation: We develop an efficient and effective approach to seamlessly integrate VSLs as conditional guidance into pre-trained diffusion models, enabling VSL-grounded video generation in a training-free manner. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SpA2V excels in generating realistic videos with semantic and spatial alignment to the input audios.
item.dc:creator: Kien T. Pham, Yingqing He, Yazhou Xing, Qifeng Chen, Long Chen

item.title: HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni
item.description: arXiv:2601.01792v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this report, we present HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni, the first any-to-any omnimodal model in the HyperCLOVA X family that supports text, audio, and vision as both inputs and outputs. By consolidating multimodal understanding and generation into a single model rather than separate modality-specific pipelines, HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni serves as an 8B-scale omni-pathfinding point toward practical any-to-any omni assistants. At a high level, the model unifies modalities through a shared next-token prediction interface over an interleaved multimodal sequence, while vision and audio encoders inject continuous embeddings for fine-grained understanding and grounding. Empirical evaluations demonstrate competitive performance against comparably sized models across diverse input-output combinations spanning text, audio, and vision, in both Korean and English. We anticipate that the open-weight release of HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni will support a wide range of research and deployment scenarios.
item.dc:creator: NAVER Cloud HyperCLOVA X Team

item.title: Enhancing time-frequency resolution with optimal transport and barycentric fusion of multiple spectrogram
item.description: arXiv:2604.15055v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Time-frequency representations, such as the short-time Fourier transform (STFT), are fundamental tools for analyzing non-stationary signals. However, their ability to achieve sharp localization in both time and frequency is inherently limited by the Gabor-Heisenberg uncertainty principle. In this paper, we address this limitation by introducing a method to generate super-resolution spectrograms through the fusion of two or more spectrograms with varying resolutions. Specifically, we compute the super-resolution spectrogram as the barycenter of input spectrograms using optimal transport (OT) divergences. Our method does not require the input spectrograms to share the same time-frequency grid. The input spectrograms can be computed using any STFT parameters, and the resulting super-resolution spectrogram can be defined on an arbitrary user-specified grid. We explore various OT divergences based on different transportation costs. Notably, we introduce a novel transportation cost that preserves time-frequency geometry while significantly reducing computational complexity compared to standard Wasserstein barycenters. We adopt the unbalanced OT framework and derive a new block majorization-minimization algorithm for efficient barycenter computation. We validate the proposed method on controlled synthetic signals and recorded speech using both quantitative and qualitative evaluations. The results show that our approach combines the best localization properties of the input spectrograms while maintaining a smooth energy distribution, and preserving computational efficiency.
item.dc:creator: David Valdivia, Elsa Cazelles, C\'edric F\'evotte

item.title: Separate First, Fuse Later: Mitigating Cross-Modal Interference in Audio-Visual LLMs Reasoning with Modality-Specific Chain-of-Thought
item.description: arXiv:2605.09906v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Audio and vision provide complementary evidence for audio-visual question answering, yet current audio-visual large language models may suffer from cross-modal interference: information from one modality misguides the interpretation of another, thereby inducing hallucinations. We attribute this issue to uncontrolled cross-modal interactions during intermediate reasoning. To mitigate this, we propose Separate First, Fuse Later (SFFL), an audio-visual reasoning framework designed to reduce cross-modal interference. SFFL enforces modality-specific chain-of-thought reasoning, producing separate audio and visual reasoning traces and integrating evidence for answering. We construct modality-preference labels via a data pipeline under different modality input settings. We use these labels as an auxiliary reward in reinforcement learning to encourage a instance-dependent preference for modality cues when answering. We further introduce a modality-specific reasoning mechanism that preserves modality isolation during the separated reasoning stage while enabling full access to cross-modal information at the evidence fusion stage. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in both accuracy and robustness, yielding an average relative gain of 5.16\% on general AVQA benchmarks and 11.17\% on a cross-modal hallucination benchmark.
item.dc:creator: Xuanchen Li, Yuheng Lu, Chenrui Cui, Tianrui Wang, Zikang Huang, Yu Jiang, Long Zhou, Longbiao Wang, Jianwu Dang

item.title: Language models represent more about emphasis than they can tell you
item.description: arXiv:2611.25808v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Prosodic prominence can largely be predicted from text, but part of it depends on how the speaker reads the sentence. We examine how much information about emphasis language models recover from text, whether they can report it when asked, and what the speech signal adds. Using English speech data with automatically derived word-level emphasis labels, we compare frozen and fine-tuned text models, prompted large language models (LLMs) and speech models on the same words. The text models end within about one point of each other, at best 68.8% on the 3-way task, and make many of the same errors. With the prompts we tested, the LLMs do no better than a word-majority baseline, even with 500 examples. While LLM responses contain some contextual information, they contain less than linear probes find in the model representations, and the gap does not close when the answers are recalibrated or the question is asked differently. The best speech model reaches 84.7%. We argue that text determines only part of the emphasis, and that the rest has to be heard. LLMs encode what the text determines, but prompting reveals only part of it: LLMs represent more about where the emphasis falls than they tell us.
